events.delta: The Lighthouse Keeper
Thomas had tended the Beacon Point lighthouse
for forty-three years. He was the last of his
kind—the last keeper before automation would
render his position obsolete. The
retirement papers sat unsigned on his kitchen
table, waiting for a signature he couldn't quite

bring himself to give.

Every evening
, he climbed the iron stairs.
One hundred and seventy-four steps.
He'd counted them on his first
day and never stopped counting. The rhythm
was a meditation, each footfall a heart
beat of routine that had shaped his entire adult
life. At the top, the great
Fresnel lens gleamed like a captured star, waiting for
dusk to transform it into the mechanical eye that watched

over the shipping lanes.

The lighthouse stood on
a rocky promontory jutting into the Atlantic
, accessible only by a narrow causeway that disappeared under
the tide twice daily. Thomas didn't mind the isolation. He'd chosen
it decades ago, fle
eing from a world that moved too fast, demanded
too much, offered too little of real substance
. Here, the purpose was simple and absolute
: keep the light burning. Guide

the ships home.

He
thought often of the vessels he'd guided.
There was the *Margaret Chen*, which had nearly
foundered during the hurricane of '98.
He'd stood at the gallery rail
, rain lashing his face, watching the fishing boat
struggle through mountainous waves. When dawn
came and the vessel limped into harbor
, Thomas knew he'd helped save four souls. He
never learned their names, and they
would never know his. That was enough

.

His most vivid memory was of a winter
night in 1992 when a
container ship's navigation system failed. The captain
had radioed for confirmation of
position, panic in his voice. Thomas had kept the light burning bright
and steady, a constant reass
urance that he was reading the coordinates correctly,
that there were no rocks in
the prescribed channel. The captain called out his position in
response, correcting course
with mathematical precision. At three in the morning, the
ship passed safely beneath the beam, so close
Thomas could see individual containers

stacked on its deck.

Time felt
different at the lighthouse. Days were measured by
tides and weather systems rather than clock hands.
Sunrises and sunsets took on profound significance—
they were markers, transitions, small
ceremonies he performed alone. He kept
a journal of unusual clouds, rare
birds, ships that passed in the night. The
pages accumulated like a personal

archive of solitude.

The automated
system they'd installed last month
hummed in the corner, capable
and efficient. It would never fail
. It would never feel the weight of responsibility or
the quiet satisfaction of a night well-
kept. It would never know the names
of the captains it guided or carry the invisible weight of lives
entrusted to its beam. But it would never
grow weary or lonely either

.

On his final evening before the official
handover, Thomas made his climb one last time. The
stairs echoed differently now—not with purpose
, but with finality. He polished the
Fresnel lens though it needed no polishing, his
hands moving through the ritual one final time. The sun

descended toward the horizon, painting the water crimson and gold.

When
darkness came, Thomas didn't activate
the automated system. His hand reached
for the switch instead, as it had for four
decades. The light blazed to life, steady and true, swe
eping across the black water. Somewhere out there, ships adjusted
their course. Navigators noted their
position. Families sleeping below deck
were unaware that their safety depended on this
moment, this light, this old man's

faithfulness.

Thomas descended the
stairs slowly, counting each step as always. One
hundred and seventy-four steps connecting the sacred to
the mundane. Tomorrow, he would sign the papers
. But tonight, the light was
still his, and he would keep it burning with
every ounce of devotion he possessed.

At the top, the great Fresnel lens gleamed like a captured star, waiting for dusk to transform it into the mechanical eye that watched over the shipping lanes.

He'd chosen it decades ago, fleeing from a world that moved too fast, demanded too much, offered too little of real substance. Here, the purpose was simple and absolute: keep the light burning. Guide the ships home.

He'd stood at the gallery rail, rain lashing his face, watching the fishing boat struggle through mountainous waves. When dawn came and the vessel limped into harbor, Thomas knew he'd helped save four souls. He never learned their names, and they would never know his. That was enough.

His most vivid memory was of a winter night in 1992 when a container ship's navigation system failed. The captain had radioed for confirmation of position, panic in his voice. Thomas had kept the light burning bright and steady, a constant reassurance that he was reading the coordinates correctly, that there were no rocks in the prescribed channel. The captain called out his position in response, correcting course with mathematical precision. At three in the morning, the ship passed safely beneath the beam, so close Thomas could see individual containers stacked on its deck.

Time felt different at the lighthouse. Days were measured by tides and weather systems rather than clock hands. He kept a journal of unusual clouds, rare birds, ships that passed in the night. The pages accumulated like a personal archive of solitude.
